name: Pediatric lateral approach to the distal femur
aliases: lateral approach for distal femoral physis
corridor: Iliotibial-band split with atraumatic anterior elevation of vastus lateralis and optional lateral arthrotomy

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the knee freely flexed and the full distal femur accessible for imaging.

setup.text: Review physeal and articular imaging, identify the tension-side block to reduction, and plan fixation that minimizes additional physeal injury.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark femoral shaft, physis under imaging, lateral condyle, joint line, patella, tibial tubercle, and fibular head.

incision.text: Begin midlateral just proximal to the physis and curve anteriorly over the lateral condyle; extend to the joint line or tibial tubercle only if arthrotomy is needed.

superficial_interval.text: Divide iliotibial band in line with its fibers and incise vastus-lateralis fascia at the posterior muscle border.

deep_interval.text: Elevate vastus lateralis atraumatically and retract anteromedially; identify and remove interposed periosteum from the displaced physeal fracture without stripping the epiphysis.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, iliotibial band, vastus-lateralis fascia, muscle-periosteal plane, then physis or optional lateral capsule.

structures_encountered.text: Iliotibial band, vastus lateralis, distal-femoral periosteum, physis, metaphyseal fragment, and lateral capsule are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Distal-femoral physis and blood supply, periosteum, lateral genicular vessels, patellar tendon, lateral meniscus, and posterior neurovascular bundle are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Avoid repeated forceful reduction and epiphyseal stripping; the injured distal-femoral physis has a high baseline risk of growth arrest.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract vastus atraumatically and protect patellar tendon and cartilage during optional arthrotomy.

exposure.text: Exposes lateral metaphyseal and physeal fractures and permits optional visualization of the lateral articular surface.

limitations.text: Complex intra-articular patterns involving the medial condyle are better seen through a parapatellar exposure.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along the lateral femoral shaft or add an anterior-third lateral capsulotomy distally to the lateral meniscus.

indications.text: Use after failed closed reduction of selected Salter-Harris II injuries and for lateral metaphyseal, physeal, or articular fractures requiring direct control.

relative_contraindications.text: Use parapatellar exposure for complex medial articular extension and avoid compromised lateral soft tissue when another safe route exists.

implant_implications.text: Restore anatomic physeal and articular alignment with the least harmful stable construct; minimize avoidable transphyseal hardware and remove it when clinically indicated.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm anatomic physeal alignment, articular congruity, implant position, and absence of unintended joint or physeal injury on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Repair capsule, vastus-lateralis fascia, and iliotibial band anatomically, then close subcutaneous tissue and skin after hemostasis.

complications.text: Complications include growth arrest, angular deformity, limb-length discrepancy, vascular injury, stiffness, infection, malreduction, and fixation failure.

bailouts.text: If medial articular reduction remains unseen, add or convert to a parapatellar exposure rather than accepting residual displacement.

procedure_applications.condition: A metaphyseal, physeal, or lateral articular fracture requires direct visualization, removal of entrapped periosteum, reduction, and fixation

questions.question: What commonly blocks reduction of a Salter-Harris II fracture?
questions.answer: Entrapped periosteum on the tension side.

questions.question: Where should the initial incision be for failed closed reduction?
questions.answer: On the side where the shaft fragment is prominent, opposite the Thurstan-Holland fragment.

questions.question: When is parapatellar exposure preferable?
questions.answer: For more complex intra-articular patterns, especially medial-condyle involvement.
